title: Select Columns With a WHERE Filter
statement: Table Employees has columns id, name, dept, salary. Show name and salary of employees in the 'Sales' dept only.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept TEXT, salary INTEGER);
solution: SELECT name, salary FROM Employees WHERE dept = 'Sales';
approach: SELECT picks columns, WHERE picks rows. Filter before anything else.
steps: Read the stem: columns wanted = name, salary -> SELECT name, salary.
Rows wanted = dept Sales only -> WHERE dept = 'Sales'.
FROM Employees glues it: SELECT name, salary FROM Employees WHERE dept = 'Sales'.
Check: Ravi(HR) and Arjun(IT) must NOT appear; 3 Sales rows appear.
insight: SELECT vs WHERE is the first AXIS MCQ trap: SELECT picks columns, WHERE picks rows.
learn: SELECT chooses columns (projection). WHERE filters rows. Text uses single quotes.

title: Salary Range With BETWEEN
statement: Show name and salary of employees whose salary is between 50000 and 75000 inclusive, sorted by salary ascending.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, salary INTEGER);
solution: SELECT name, salary FROM Employees WHERE salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 75000 ORDER BY salary ASC;
starter:
-- name, salary where 50000..75000 inclusive, ordered by salary
SELECT name, salary FROM Employees
WHERE salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 75000
ORDER BY salary ASC;
approach: BETWEEN ... AND ... is inclusive on both ends. ORDER BY sorts the survivors.
steps: BETWEEN 50000 AND 75000 keeps 50000 and 75000 themselves (inclusive).
50000 (Ravi) and 75000 (Meena) are IN; 80000 and 45000 are OUT.
ORDER BY salary ASC sorts low to high.
Never write salary > 50000 AND salary < 75000 when the stem says inclusive — that drops the endpoints.
insight: BETWEEN is inclusive. The exam's off-by-one trap is exclusive >/< vs inclusive BETWEEN.
learn: BETWEEN a AND b keeps both endpoints. ORDER BY ... ASC sorts ascending.

title: Name Patterns With LIKE
years: AXIS Technical MCQ pool; TCS NQT repeat
statement: Show names that start with 'A'. Then the judge's hidden test checks names ending with 'esh' with a second query slot — write ONE query using LIKE that the hidden test reuses: match names starting with 'A'. (Concept: % = any length, _ = exactly one char.)
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
solution: SELECT name FROM Employees WHERE name LIKE 'A%' ORDER BY name;
starter:
-- names starting with A
SELECT name FROM Employees
WHERE name LIKE 'A%'
ORDER BY name;
approach: LIKE 'A%' = starts with A. % matches any length including zero.
steps: LIKE 'A%' -> first letter A, rest anything (Asha, Anil, A, Aarav).
Ravi and Ramesh do NOT start with A -> excluded.
'A__' would mean exactly 3 letters starting with A — different from 'A%'.
ORDER BY name keeps output deterministic for the judge.
insight: % = any length (incl. zero), _ = exactly one char. 'A%' vs 'A__' is a binary exam trap.
learn: LIKE 'A%' starts-with, LIKE '%esh' ends-with, 'A__' exactly 3 chars.

title: NULL Check: Find Missing Phones
statement: Show name of employees whose phone is missing (NULL).
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, phone TEXT);
solution: SELECT name FROM Employees WHERE phone IS NULL ORDER BY name;
starter:
-- names with missing phone
SELECT name FROM Employees
WHERE phone IS NULL
ORDER BY name;
approach: Any comparison with = NULL is never true. IS NULL is the only null test.
steps: WHERE phone = NULL matches NOTHING (UNKNOWN, filtered out) — never write it.
WHERE phone IS NULL matches Ravi and Arjun.
Empty string '' is NOT null — Meena with '' is excluded. Correct.
ORDER BY name for determinism.
insight: WHERE col = NULL is always wrong. IS NULL is the only null test (three-valued logic).
learn: NULL means unknown. = NULL is never true; use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.

title: Top 2 Earners (ORDER BY + LIMIT)
statement: Show name and salary of the top 2 earners (highest salary first).
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, salary INTEGER);
solution: SELECT name, salary FROM Employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 2;
starter:
-- top 2 earners, highest first
SELECT name, salary FROM Employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 2;
approach: ORDER BY salary DESC sorts high to low; LIMIT 2 caps at two rows.
steps: ORDER BY salary DESC puts 90000s first.
LIMIT 2 keeps only the first two rows.
Ties (two 90000s) both fit in top 2 here; with LIMIT 1 the tie-break would need a second ORDER key.
SQL Server uses TOP 2, Oracle ROWNUM — AXIS uses LIMIT (MySQL/Postgres style).
insight: ORDER BY sorts after filtering; LIMIT caps last. DESC = high to low.
learn: ORDER BY col DESC + LIMIT n = top-n pattern. LIMIT runs last.

title: Highest Salary (MAX)
years: FACE Prep PYQ: 'Which query fetches highest salary?'
statement: Return the highest salary in Employees as column max_sal.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, salary INTEGER);
solution: SELECT MAX(salary) AS max_sal FROM Employees;
starter:
-- highest salary as max_sal
SELECT MAX(salary) AS max_sal FROM Employees;
approach: MAX() collapses all rows to one value. Alias it as asked.
steps: MAX(salary) scans all rows, keeps the biggest: 90000.
AS max_sal renames the output column — the judge checks the column name.
WHERE salary = MAX() is INVALID — aggregates cannot sit in WHERE.
One row, one column is the whole answer.
insight: FACE PYQ answer: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees. MAX() never goes in WHERE.
learn: MAX/MIN/SUM/AVG/COUNT collapse many rows to one. Aliases rename output columns.

title: Second Highest Salary
years: Accenture DA interview Q4; classic repeat 2021-2025
statement: Return the second highest DISTINCT salary as column second_max. Duplicates of the max do not count.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, salary INTEGER);
solution: SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_max FROM Employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employees);
approach: Inner query finds the max; outer takes MAX of everything below it. Duplicates of max are excluded by <.
steps: Inner: SELECT MAX(salary) = 90000.
Outer keeps rows with salary < 90000: 60000, 75000 (both 90000s dropped).
MAX of survivors = 75000 = second highest DISTINCT.
Alternative: SELECT DISTINCT salary ... ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1.
insight: Second-highest-DISTINCT is the most-asked Accenture SQL interview query. < max drops duplicate maxes.
learn: Subquery in WHERE computes the max first; outer query filters below it.

title: Average Project Cost Per Year
statement: Table Projects(project_id, yr, cost). Return each yr and its average cost as avg_cost, ordered by yr.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Projects(project_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, yr INTEGER, cost INTEGER);
solution: SELECT yr, AVG(cost) AS avg_cost FROM Projects GROUP BY yr ORDER BY yr;
starter:
-- yr and average cost per year
SELECT yr, AVG(cost) AS avg_cost FROM Projects
GROUP BY yr
ORDER BY yr;
approach: GROUP BY yr makes one bucket per year; AVG(cost) reduces each bucket to one number.
steps: GROUP BY yr -> bucket 2021 (3 rows), bucket 2022 (3 rows).
ORDER BY yr for determinism. Every SELECT col is grouped or aggregated -> valid.
insight: DataLemur Q8 verbatim pattern. GROUP BY buckets, aggregate reduces.
learn: GROUP BY defines buckets; AVG/SUM/COUNT reduce each bucket to one row.

title: Top 3 Selling Products
pattern: JOIN + GROUP BY + SUM + ORDER + LIMIT
statement: Tables Products(product_id, product_name) and Sales(sale_id, product_id, amount). Return the top 3 product_name by total sales with column total_sales, highest first.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Products(product_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, product_name TEXT); CREATE TABLE Sales(sale_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, product_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER);
seedSQL: INSERT INTO Products VALUES (1,'Keyboard'),(2,'Mouse'),(3,'Monitor'),(4,'Cable'); INSERT INTO Sales VALUES (1,1,100),(2,1,200),(3,2,500),(4,3,400),(5,3,100),(6,2,100),(7,4,50);
solution: SELECT p.product_name, SUM(s.amount) AS total_sales FROM Products p JOIN Sales s ON s.product_id = p.product_id GROUP BY p.product_name ORDER BY total_sales DESC LIMIT 3;
starter:
-- top 3 products by total sales
SELECT p.product_name, SUM(s.amount) AS total_sales
FROM Products p JOIN Sales s ON s.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY p.product_name
ORDER BY total_sales DESC
LIMIT 3;
approach: JOIN lines up names with amounts; GROUP BY product collapses; SUM totals; ORDER+LIMIT takes top 3.
steps: JOIN Products-Sales ON product_id: every sale now carries its product_name.
GROUP BY product_name -> one row per product.
SUM(amount): Keyboard 300, Mouse 600, Monitor 500, Cable 50.
ORDER BY total_sales DESC LIMIT 3 -> Mouse 600, Monitor 500, Keyboard 300.
insight: Real Accenture DA question. JOIN+GROUP+SUM+ORDER+LIMIT is one inseparable pipeline.
learn: JOIN first, GROUP BY product, SUM the measure, ORDER DESC, LIMIT n.

title: Customers With More Than 3 Orders
years: Accenture DA live coding (LinkedIn 2025): '>3 orders in 6 months'
statement: Table Orders(order_id, customer_id). Return customer_id and order_count for customers with more than 3 orders, highest count first.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Orders(order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER);
solution: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count FROM Orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 3 ORDER BY order_count DESC;
starter:
-- customers with >3 orders
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM Orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3
ORDER BY order_count DESC;
approach: GROUP BY customer buckets orders; HAVING filters buckets on the COUNT aggregate.
steps: GROUP BY customer_id: 101->4, 102->2, 103->5.
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3 keeps 101 and 103 (102 dropped).
WHERE COUNT(*) > 3 would be INVALID — aggregates invisible in WHERE.
ORDER BY order_count DESC: 103(5) then 101(4).
insight: HAVING filters groups after aggregation; WHERE cannot see aggregates. The defining trap.
learn: WHERE filters rows before groups; HAVING filters groups after (on COUNT/SUM/AVG).

title: Departments With 2+ Employees
statement: Table Employees(id, name, dept). Return dept and headcount for departments with at least 2 employees, ordered by headcount desc.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept TEXT);
solution: SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS headcount FROM Employees GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 ORDER BY headcount DESC;
starter:
-- dept + headcount where >= 2
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM Employees
GROUP BY dept
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY headcount DESC;
approach: Bucket by dept, count rows per bucket, keep buckets with 2+.
steps: Buckets: Sales 3, HR 1, IT 1.
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 keeps Sales only.
COUNT(*) counts rows even with NULLs; COUNT(col) would skip nulls.
ORDER BY headcount DESC.
insight: Same skeleton as customers>3: GROUP BY bucket, HAVING on COUNT.
learn: COUNT(*) counts rows (even NULLs); COUNT(col) counts non-null values.

title: Second Highest Salary Per Department
years: Accenture DA interview: 'second highest in EACH department'
statement: Tables Employees(id, name, dept, salary). Return dept and second_max (second highest DISTINCT salary within that dept), one row per dept, ordered by dept.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept TEXT, salary INTEGER);
solution: SELECT dept, MAX(salary) AS second_max FROM Employees e WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employees WHERE dept = e.dept) GROUP BY dept ORDER BY dept;
starter:
-- dept + second highest distinct salary per dept
SELECT dept, MAX(salary) AS second_max
FROM Employees e
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employees WHERE dept = e.dept)
GROUP BY dept
ORDER BY dept;
approach: Correlated subquery finds each row's own-dept max; outer keeps salaries below it, MAX per dept = second highest.
steps: For Sales rows, inner finds Sales max 300; survivors 100,200 -> MAX 200.
For HR rows, inner finds HR max 500; survivor 400 -> MAX 400.
IT has one salary: nothing below max -> IT row vanishes (no second max exists).
Correlation WHERE dept = e.dept (outer ref inside) is the tell: runs per outer row.
insight: Per-group max needs correlation (outer dept inside). Non-correlated = overall max, different answer.
learn: Correlated subquery references the outer row (e.dept) and runs per row; non-correlated runs once.

title: Employees With Departments (INNER JOIN)
years: AXIS coding SQL slot archetype; GfG ASE interview
statement: Tables Employees(id, name, dept_id) and Departments(id, dept_name). Show name and dept_name for employees that HAVE a matching department, ordered by name.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept_id INTEGER); CREATE TABLE Departments(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, dept_name TEXT);
seedSQL: INSERT INTO Employees VALUES (1,'Asha',10),(2,'Ravi',20),(3,'Meena',NULL),(4,'Arjun',99); INSERT INTO Departments VALUES (10,'Sales'),(20,'HR'),(30,'IT');
hiddenSeedSQL: INSERT INTO Employees VALUES (10,'Kabir',30),(11,'Nina',NULL); INSERT INTO Departments VALUES (30,'Ops'),(40,'Legal');
solution: SELECT e.name, d.dept_name FROM Employees e INNER JOIN Departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id ORDER BY e.name;
starter:
-- name + dept_name for matched rows only
SELECT e.name, d.dept_name
FROM Employees e INNER JOIN Departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id
ORDER BY e.name;
approach: INNER JOIN keeps only rows matching on both sides. Meena(NULL) and Arjun(99) drop out.
steps: ON e.dept_id = d.id is the match condition.
Asha 10->Sales match; Ravi 20->HR match.
Meena dept NULL matches nothing -> dropped. Arjun 99 has no dept 99 -> dropped.
Dept IT(30) with no employee -> dropped (no match on left).
insight: INNER = overlap only. The Venn centre. Non-matches on either side vanish.
learn: INNER JOIN keeps only matches. ON is the match condition.

title: ALL Employees With Department If Any (LEFT JOIN)
years: AXIS coding SQL slot archetype; Top-25 Q1
statement: Same tables. Show ALL employees with dept_name where present (NULL when missing), ordered by name.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept_id INTEGER); CREATE TABLE Departments(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, dept_name TEXT);
seedSQL: INSERT INTO Employees VALUES (1,'Asha',10),(2,'Ravi',20),(3,'Meena',NULL),(4,'Arjun',99); INSERT INTO Departments VALUES (10,'Sales'),(20,'HR');
hiddenSeedSQL: INSERT INTO Employees VALUES (10,'Kabir',NULL),(11,'Nina',50); INSERT INTO Departments VALUES (50,'Ops');
solution: SELECT e.name, d.dept_name FROM Employees e LEFT JOIN Departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id ORDER BY e.name;
starter:
-- all employees, dept where present
SELECT e.name, d.dept_name
FROM Employees e LEFT JOIN Departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id
ORDER BY e.name;
approach: LEFT JOIN preserves every left row; right fills NULL on no match.
steps: Asha->Sales, Ravi->HR (matches).
Meena NULL and Arjun 99 have no match -> kept with dept_name NULL.
4 rows out (vs 2 for INNER). That row-count gap is the exam's favourite distinguisher.
WHERE d.dept_name = 'Sales' after this LEFT would kill the NULL rows -> silently becomes INNER.
insight: 'All employees even if no department' -> LEFT JOIN from Employees. ON shapes join, WHERE filters after.
learn: LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows; missing right side becomes NULL.

title: LEFT JOIN: Filter Inside ON, Not WHERE
statement: Show ALL employees with their dept_name but only attach Sales departments (other employees show NULL, yet still appear). Ordered by name.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept_id INTEGER); CREATE TABLE Departments(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, dept_name TEXT);
seedSQL: INSERT INTO Employees VALUES (1,'Asha',10),(2,'Ravi',20),(3,'Meena',NULL); INSERT INTO Departments VALUES (10,'Sales'),(20,'HR');
hiddenSeedSQL: INSERT INTO Employees VALUES (10,'K',100),(11,'L',200),(12,'M',NULL); INSERT INTO Departments VALUES (100,'Sales'),(200,'Ops');
solution: SELECT e.name, d.dept_name FROM Employees e LEFT JOIN Departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id AND d.dept_name = 'Sales' ORDER BY e.name;
starter:
-- all employees; attach dept only if Sales
SELECT e.name, d.dept_name
FROM Employees e LEFT JOIN Departments d ON e.dept_id = d.id AND d.dept_name = 'Sales'
ORDER BY e.name;
approach: Put the Sales filter in ON: non-Sales matches become NULL but rows survive. WHERE would delete them.
steps: Asha 10 Sales: ON matches fully -> Sales attached.
Ravi 20 HR: AND dept='Sales' fails -> kept with NULL (still appears!).
Meena NULL -> NULL.
If instead WHERE d.dept_name='Sales': NULL rows filtered out -> only Asha. That is the trap.
insight: OUTER + WHERE on outer column = silently INNER. Filter the preserved side in ON.
learn: ON decides the match; WHERE prunes the joined result afterwards.

title: Employees Earning More Than Their Managers
statement: Table Employees(id, name, salary, manager_id) where manager_id points to another employee's id. Show names of employees earning more than their own manager, ordered by name.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, salary INTEGER, manager_id INTEGER);
solution: SELECT e.name FROM Employees e JOIN Employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id WHERE e.salary > m.salary ORDER BY e.name;
starter:
-- employees earning more than their manager
SELECT e.name
FROM Employees e JOIN Employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary
ORDER BY e.name;
approach: SELF JOIN: same table twice with aliases e (employee) and m (manager).
steps: Aliases e and m let one table play two roles.
Bob 80000 vs Alice 100000 -> no. Carol 120000 vs Alice 100000 -> YES.
Dave 70000 vs Bob 80000 -> no. Alice has no manager (NULL) -> no match -> excluded.
WHERE compares the pair's salaries.
insight: Manager problems = SELF JOIN with aliases. e.manager_id = m.id is the skeleton.
learn: SELF JOIN joins a table to itself via aliases (employee vs manager).

title: AXIS Archetype: Customer Orders With Product Names
statement: Tables Customers(customer_id, name), Orders(order_id, customer_id, product_id, qty), Products(product_id, product_name, price). Show customer name, product_name, qty, and line total (qty*price) as total for every order, ordered by order_id.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Customers(customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE Orders(order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, product_id INTEGER, qty INTEGER); CREATE TABLE Products(product_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, product_name TEXT, price INTEGER);
seedSQL: INSERT INTO Customers VALUES (1,'Asha'),(2,'Ravi'); INSERT INTO Products VALUES (10,'Pen',100),(20,'Book',250); INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (100,1,10,2),(101,2,20,1),(102,1,20,3);
hiddenSeedSQL: INSERT INTO Customers VALUES (5,'K'),(6,'L'); INSERT INTO Products VALUES (50,'Desk',1000),(60,'Lamp',500); INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (200,5,50,1),(201,6,60,4);
solution: SELECT c.name, p.product_name, o.qty, (o.qty * p.price) AS total FROM Orders o JOIN Customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN Products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id ORDER BY o.order_id;
starter:
-- customer, product, qty, total per order
SELECT c.name, p.product_name, o.qty, (o.qty * p.price) AS total
FROM Orders o
JOIN Customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN Products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id
ORDER BY o.order_id;
approach: Chain two JOINs from the fact table (Orders) to each dimension. Compute qty*price inline.
steps: Orders is the centre: one FK to Customers, one to Products.
First JOIN attaches customer names; second attaches product names+prices.
qty*price AS total computes the line value per row (no GROUP BY needed).
ORDER BY o.order_id keeps judge order deterministic.
insight: This 3-table chain IS the AXIS SQL coding slot. Centre fact + two dimension JOINs.
learn: Chain JOINs: fact table JOIN dim1 ON fk1 JOIN dim2 ON fk2.

title: Employee Count Per Department, Including Empty
statement: Tables Departments(id, dept_name), Employees(id, name, dept_id). Show every dept_name with its headcount (0 for empty depts), ordered by dept_name.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Departments(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, dept_name TEXT); CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept_id INTEGER);
seedSQL: INSERT INTO Departments VALUES (10,'Sales'),(20,'HR'),(30,'IT'); INSERT INTO Employees VALUES (1,'A',10),(2,'B',10),(3,'C',20);
hiddenSeedSQL: INSERT INTO Departments VALUES (1,'A'),(2,'B'); INSERT INTO Employees VALUES (10,'X',1);
solution: SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(e.id) AS headcount FROM Departments d LEFT JOIN Employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id GROUP BY d.dept_name ORDER BY d.dept_name;
starter:
-- every dept + headcount incl. zeros
SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(e.id) AS headcount
FROM Departments d LEFT JOIN Employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.dept_name
ORDER BY d.dept_name;
approach: LEFT from Departments preserves empty ones; COUNT(e.id) counts matches (NULL -> 0).
steps: LEFT from Departments: IT(30) survives with NULL employee side.
COUNT(e.id) ignores NULLs -> IT headcount 0. (COUNT(*) would wrongly give 1!)
Sales 2, HR 1, IT 0.
INNER would drop IT entirely — the classic wrong answer.
insight: Zero-count needs LEFT + COUNT(right.id). COUNT(*) counts the NULL row — use COUNT(col).
learn: COUNT(col) skips NULLs (gives 0 for empty groups); COUNT(*) counts rows.

title: Orders With Customer Names in 2024
statement: Tables Customers(customer_id, name), Orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date TEXT 'YYYY-MM-DD'). Show order_id, name, order_date for orders in 2024, ordered by order_id.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Customers(customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE Orders(order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, order_date TEXT);
seedSQL: INSERT INTO Customers VALUES (1,'Asha'),(2,'Ravi'); INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (100,1,'2024-03-01'),(101,2,'2023-12-31'),(102,1,'2024-07-15');
hiddenSeedSQL: INSERT INTO Customers VALUES (5,'K'); INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (200,5,'2024-01-01'),(201,5,'2025-01-01');
solution: SELECT o.order_id, c.name, o.order_date FROM Orders o JOIN Customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_date LIKE '2024%' ORDER BY o.order_id;
starter:
-- 2024 orders with customer names
SELECT o.order_id, c.name, o.order_date
FROM Orders o JOIN Customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_date LIKE '2024%'
ORDER BY o.order_id;
approach: JOIN for names; WHERE on the date string filters the year (SQLite-friendly).
steps: JOIN attaches names to orders.
Dates stored 'YYYY-MM-DD': LIKE '2024%' keeps 2024 rows.
2023-12-31 drops out.
ORDER BY order_id.
insight: SQLite date-as-text + LIKE 'YYYY%' is the portable year filter (no DATEADD dialect issues).
learn: Store dates as 'YYYY-MM-DD' text; filter years with LIKE 'YYYY%'.

title: Salary Above Company Average
statement: Show name and salary of employees earning more than the company average, ordered by name.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, salary INTEGER);
solution: SELECT name, salary FROM Employees WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM Employees) ORDER BY name;
starter:
-- above company average
SELECT name, salary FROM Employees
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM Employees)
ORDER BY name;
approach: Inner query runs once (overall AVG); outer compares each row to it.
steps: Outer keeps salary > 60000: Meena 80000 only (Asha equals, not greater).
Non-correlated: no outer reference inside -> runs once.
Swap to correlated (dept = e.dept) and the answer becomes per-dept — different result.
insight: No outer ref inside = runs once = overall average. The scope decides the result.
learn: Subquery in WHERE runs first; outer query uses its single value.

title: Salary Above Own Department Average
years: AXIS synthesis favourite: overall vs per-group
statement: Show name, dept, salary of employees earning more than their OWN department's average, ordered by name.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept TEXT, salary INTEGER);
solution: SELECT e.name, e.dept, e.salary FROM Employees e WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM Employees WHERE dept = e.dept) ORDER BY e.name;
starter:
-- above own-dept average
SELECT e.name, e.dept, e.salary FROM Employees e
WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM Employees WHERE dept = e.dept)
ORDER BY e.name;
approach: dept = e.dept (outer ref) makes it correlated: average recomputed per row's dept.
steps: Sales avg = 200: C 300 > 200 YES; A,B no.
HR avg = 300: D 500 YES; E 100 no.
Answer: C, D. Overall-avg version would give different rows (only D).
dept = e.dept inside is the correlation tell.
insight: Same skeleton as above-average, but the outer ref flips overall -> per-group. Exam shows both.
learn: Outer reference (e.dept) inside = correlated = per-row recomputation.

title: Subject Matter Experts (UNION + HAVING)
years: DataLemur Accenture Q1 (2025); LinkedIn SME post
statement: Table WorkExp(employee_id, domain, years_of_experience). An SME has 8+ years in a single domain OR 12+ total years across exactly two domains. Return distinct employee_id of SMEs, ordered ascending.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE WorkExp(employee_id INTEGER, domain TEXT, years_of_experience INTEGER);
seedSQL: INSERT INTO WorkExp VALUES (101,'Digital Transformation',9),(102,'Supply Chain',6),(102,'IoT',7),(103,'Change Management',4),(104,'DevOps',5),(104,'Cloud Migration',5),(104,'Agile Transformation',5);
solution: SELECT employee_id FROM WorkExp WHERE years_of_experience >= 8 UNION SELECT employee_id FROM WorkExp GROUP BY employee_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT domain) = 2 AND SUM(years_of_experience) >= 12 ORDER BY employee_id;
starter:
-- SME ids: 8+ single domain OR 12+ across exactly two
SELECT employee_id FROM WorkExp WHERE years_of_experience >= 8
UNION
SELECT employee_id FROM WorkExp GROUP BY employee_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT domain) = 2 AND SUM(years_of_experience) >= 12
ORDER BY employee_id;
approach: Two SME rules = two queries UNIONed (UNION dedupes). Second rule is GROUP+HAVING on count and sum.
steps: Rule 1 (WHERE >= 8): 101 (9) qualifies. Nobody else has a single 8+ row.
Rule 2 (GROUP+HAVING): 102 has 2 domains totalling 13 >= 12 YES; 103 one domain no; 104 three domains no.
UNION merges {101} + {102} = 101, 102 (deduped).
UNION (not UNION ALL) removes the duplicate if someone qualifies both ways.
insight: Real Accenture PYQ. WHERE for single-row rule, GROUP+HAVING for multi-row rule, UNION to combine.
learn: UNION merges two result sets and removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them.

title: Products Ever Sold (IN Subquery)
statement: Tables Products(product_id, product_name), Sales(sale_id, product_id). Show product_name of products that appear in Sales at least once, ordered by name.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Products(product_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, product_name TEXT); CREATE TABLE Sales(sale_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, product_id INTEGER);
seedSQL: INSERT INTO Products VALUES (1,'Pen'),(2,'Book'),(3,'Desk'); INSERT INTO Sales VALUES (1,1),(2,1),(3,3);
hiddenSeedSQL: INSERT INTO Products VALUES (10,'A'),(11,'B'); INSERT INTO Sales VALUES (20,11);
solution: SELECT product_name FROM Products WHERE product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM Sales) ORDER BY product_name;
starter:
-- products with >=1 sale
SELECT product_name FROM Products
WHERE product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM Sales)
ORDER BY product_name;
approach: IN checks membership of each product_id in the sales list.
steps: Subquery list: {1, 1, 3} -> membership {1,3}.
Pen(1) YES, Book(2) NO, Desk(3) YES.
Ordered: Desk, Pen.
= ANY behaves like IN; EXISTS checks presence differently.
insight: IN = 'is this value in the subquery list'. The membership operator.
learn: WHERE x IN (subquery) = membership test against the subquery's values.

title: Never-Sold Products (NOT IN vs NULL Trap)
statement: Same tables, but the hidden dataset's Sales contains a NULL product_id (dirty data). Show product_name of products with zero sales, ordered by name. Your query must survive the NULL row.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Products(product_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, product_name TEXT); CREATE TABLE Sales(sale_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, product_id INTEGER);
seedSQL: INSERT INTO Products VALUES (1,'Pen'),(2,'Book'),(3,'Desk'); INSERT INTO Sales VALUES (1,1),(2,NULL),(3,3);
hiddenSeedSQL: INSERT INTO Products VALUES (10,'A'),(11,'B'),(12,'C'); INSERT INTO Sales VALUES (20,10),(21,NULL);
solution: SELECT product_name FROM Products WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Sales WHERE Sales.product_id = Products.product_id) ORDER BY product_name;
starter:
-- products with zero sales (NULL-safe)
SELECT product_name FROM Products
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Sales WHERE Sales.product_id = Products.product_id)
ORDER BY product_name;
approach: NOT IN with a NULL in the list matches nothing (UNKNOWN). NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe.
steps: Naive NOT IN (1, NULL, 3): Book vs NULL -> UNKNOWN -> filtered -> EMPTY answer. Wrong.
NOT EXISTS checks per product: Book has no matching sale row (NULL never equals 2) -> kept. Correct.
Answer: Book (visible) / B,C (hidden).
Rule: dirty/nullable columns -> NOT EXISTS, never NOT IN.
insight: NOT IN (NULL) matches nothing. NOT EXISTS is the NULL-safe negation. Famous trap.
learn: NOT IN + NULL = UNKNOWN = no rows. NOT EXISTS handles NULL correctly.

title: UNION vs UNION ALL Row Counts
statement: Tables Auditors(name) and Mentors(name). List all distinct names appearing in EITHER table, ordered by name.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Auditors(name TEXT); CREATE TABLE Mentors(name TEXT);
seedSQL: INSERT INTO Auditors VALUES ('Asha'),('Ravi'),('Asha'); INSERT INTO Mentors VALUES ('Ravi'),('Meena');
hiddenSeedSQL: INSERT INTO Auditors VALUES ('X'),('Y'); INSERT INTO Mentors VALUES ('Y'),('Z'),('Z');
solution: SELECT name FROM Auditors UNION SELECT name FROM Mentors ORDER BY name;
starter:
-- distinct names from either table
SELECT name FROM Auditors
UNION
SELECT name FROM Mentors
ORDER BY name;
approach: UNION merges and dedupes. UNION ALL would keep duplicates (5 rows vs 3).
steps: Combined multiset: Asha,Asha,Ravi + Ravi,Meena.
UNION dedupes -> Asha, Meena, Ravi (3 rows).
UNION ALL would keep 5 rows (dupes kept, faster).
Both sides need same column count/types.
insight: UNION = distinct merge; UNION ALL = keep duplicates (faster, no sort-dedupe).
learn: UNION removes duplicates between two queries; UNION ALL keeps them.

title: Salary Bands With CASE
statement: Show name, salary, and band where band is 'High' if salary >= 80000, 'Mid' if >= 50000, else 'Low'. Ordered by name.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, salary INTEGER);
solution: SELECT name, salary, CASE WHEN salary >= 80000 THEN 'High' WHEN salary >= 50000 THEN 'Mid' ELSE 'Low' END AS band FROM Employees ORDER BY name;
starter:
-- name, salary, High/Mid/Low band
SELECT name, salary,
CASE WHEN salary >= 80000 THEN 'High' WHEN salary >= 50000 THEN 'Mid' ELSE 'Low' END AS band
FROM Employees
ORDER BY name;
approach: CASE evaluates WHENs in order; first true wins. 80000 must come before 50000.
steps: Ravi 60000: first WHEN false, second >= 50000 true -> Mid.
Meena 40000 -> ELSE Low.
Order of WHENs matters: if 50000-check came first, 90000 would wrongly be Mid.
insight: CASE = if-else per row. Put the strictest threshold first.
learn: CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END builds a computed column per row.

title: Give Sales a 10% Raise (UPDATE)
statement: Table Employees(id, name, dept, salary). Raise Sales salaries by 10% (salary = salary * 1.1). The judge checks the table AFTER your statement runs.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept TEXT, salary INTEGER);
solution: UPDATE Employees SET salary = salary * 1.1 WHERE dept = 'Sales';
starter:
-- 10% raise for Sales only
UPDATE Employees SET salary = salary * 1.1 WHERE dept = 'Sales';
verify: SELECT name, salary FROM Employees ORDER BY name;
approach: UPDATE changes existing rows; WHERE restricts to Sales. No WHERE = everyone raised (wrong).
steps: SET salary = salary * 1.1 computes per row.
WHERE dept = 'Sales' restricts: Asha 11000, Meena 22000, Ravi stays 10000.
Forgetting WHERE raises everyone -> hidden test fails.
Judge runs your UPDATE then reads the table with the verify query.
insight: UPDATE without WHERE updates everything. The WHERE is the whole question.
learn: UPDATE t SET col = expr WHERE filter — changes existing rows.

title: Delete Retired Employees (DELETE)
statement: Table Employees(id, name, status). Delete rows with status 'retired'. Judge checks remaining rows.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, status TEXT);
solution: DELETE FROM Employees WHERE status = 'retired';
starter:
-- remove retired rows
DELETE FROM Employees WHERE status = 'retired';
verify: SELECT name, status FROM Employees ORDER BY name;
approach: DELETE removes rows matching WHERE. TRUNCATE would wipe all (wrong).
steps: WHERE status='retired' matches Ravi only.
After: Asha active, Meena active.
DELETE without WHERE empties the table -> fail.
TRUNCATE clears all fast but cannot filter — wrong here.
insight: DELETE + WHERE removes matching rows. No WHERE = all rows gone.
learn: DELETE FROM t WHERE filter — removes matching rows only.

title: Rank Employees by Salary (Window Function)
statement: Show name, salary, and rnk where rnk is the RANK() by salary descending (ties share a rank, next rank skips). Ordered by rnk, then name.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, salary INTEGER);
solution: SELECT name, salary, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk FROM Employees ORDER BY rnk, name;
starter:
-- name, salary, rank by salary desc
SELECT name, salary, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
FROM Employees
ORDER BY rnk, name;
approach: RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) numbers rows by salary; equal salaries share rank with a gap after.
steps: 90000,90000 tie -> both rnk 1; next (75000) is rnk 3 (gap).
ROW_NUMBER would give 1,2,3,4 (no shared rank) — wrong here.
DENSE_RANK would give 1,1,2,3 (no gap) — wrong here.
ORDER BY rnk, name for determinism.
insight: RANK shares + skips; DENSE_RANK shares, no skip; ROW_NUMBER never shares. Exam tests the gap.
learn: RANK() OVER (ORDER BY x DESC) ranks rows; ties share rank with a gap.

title: Monthly Running Total (CTE)
statement: Table Sales(sale_id, month TEXT, amount). Show month, monthly total as mtotal, and running total as running, ordered by month. Use a CTE.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Sales(sale_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, month TEXT, amount INTEGER);
solution: WITH M AS (SELECT month, SUM(amount) AS mtotal FROM Sales GROUP BY month) SELECT month, mtotal, SUM(mtotal) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS running FROM M ORDER BY month;
starter:
-- monthly + running totals via CTE
WITH M AS (SELECT month, SUM(amount) AS mtotal FROM Sales GROUP BY month)
SELECT month, mtotal, SUM(mtotal) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS running
FROM M
ORDER BY month;
approach: CTE M aggregates per month; outer window SUM OVER (ORDER BY month) accumulates.
steps: Window SUM over ordered months: 300, 450, 750.
CTE = named temp result (WITH M AS ...); readable + reusable.
Without ORDER BY in OVER, the running frame is undefined.
insight: CTE for the grain (per-month), window for the accumulation. Two-layer pattern.
learn: WITH x AS (...) names a temp result; SUM(y) OVER (ORDER BY m) accumulates.

title: Average Project Duration in Days
statement: Table Projects(project_id, start_date TEXT 'YYYY-MM-DD', end_date TEXT). Return the average duration in days as avg_days (single row).
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Projects(project_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, start_date TEXT, end_date TEXT);
solution: SELECT AVG(JULIANDAY(end_date) - JULIANDAY(start_date)) AS avg_days FROM Projects;
starter:
-- average duration in days
SELECT AVG(JULIANDAY(end_date) - JULIANDAY(start_date)) AS avg_days FROM Projects;
approach: JULIANDAY converts dates to day numbers; subtraction = duration; AVG averages.
steps: Row 1: Apr 1 - Jan 1 = 90 days. Row 2: May 15 - Feb 15 = 89 days.
Dates must be 'YYYY-MM-DD' for JULIANDAY.
Dialect note: SQL Server uses DATEDIFF, Postgres casts ::date — SQLite uses JULIANDAY.
insight: DataLemur Q4 adapted to SQLite. JULIANDAY(end)-JULIANDAY(start) = days.
learn: JULIANDAY(d) turns a date into a day number; differences are durations.

title: Click-Through Conversion Rate
statement: Tables Views(view_id, product_id) and Carts(cart_id, product_id). Return product_id and conv_rate = 100.0 * carts / views per product, ordered by product_id. Include products with views even if zero carts.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Views(view_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, product_id INTEGER); CREATE TABLE Carts(cart_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, product_id INTEGER);
hiddenSeedSQL: INSERT INTO Views VALUES (10,301),(11,301); INSERT INTO Carts VALUES (20,301);
solution: WITH V AS (SELECT product_id, COUNT(*) AS v FROM Views GROUP BY product_id), C AS (SELECT product_id, COUNT(*) AS c FROM Carts GROUP BY product_id) SELECT V.product_id, (100.0 * COALESCE(C.c, 0) / V.v) AS conv_rate FROM V LEFT JOIN C ON V.product_id = C.product_id ORDER BY V.product_id;
starter:
-- conv_rate = 100*carts/views per product
WITH V AS (SELECT product_id, COUNT(*) AS v FROM Views GROUP BY product_id),
C AS (SELECT product_id, COUNT(*) AS c FROM Carts GROUP BY product_id)
SELECT V.product_id, (100.0 * COALESCE(C.c, 0) / V.v) AS conv_rate
FROM V LEFT JOIN C ON V.product_id = C.product_id
ORDER BY V.product_id;
approach: Two CTEs count views and carts per product; LEFT JOIN keeps zero-cart products; 100.0 forces float division.
steps: LEFT JOIN keeps products with no carts (COALESCE 0).
100.0 (not 100) avoids integer division -> 0.
insight: Real Accenture analytics Q. CTE-per-grain + LEFT JOIN + float ratio is the reporting skeleton.
learn: COALESCE(x,0) turns NULL into 0; 100.0 forces float division.

title: MOCK 1: High-Value Customers (3-Table + HAVING)
statement: Tables Customers(customer_id, name), Orders(order_id, customer_id), Payments(order_id, amount). Show name and total_spent for customers whose total exceeds 1000, ordered by total_spent desc.
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Customers(customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT); CREATE TABLE Orders(order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER); CREATE TABLE Payments(order_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER);
seedSQL: INSERT INTO Customers VALUES (1,'Asha'),(2,'Ravi'),(3,'Meena'); INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (10,1),(11,1),(12,2),(13,3); INSERT INTO Payments VALUES (10,700),(11,500),(12,400),(13,2000);
hiddenSeedSQL: INSERT INTO Customers VALUES (5,'K'),(6,'L'); INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (20,5),(21,6); INSERT INTO Payments VALUES (20,1500),(21,500);
solution: SELECT c.name, SUM(p.amount) AS total_spent FROM Customers c JOIN Orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN Payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id GROUP BY c.name HAVING SUM(p.amount) > 1000 ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
starter:
-- customers with total > 1000
SELECT c.name, SUM(p.amount) AS total_spent
FROM Customers c
JOIN Orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN Payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY c.name
HAVING SUM(p.amount) > 1000
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
approach: Two JOINs to reach amounts; GROUP BY customer; HAVING on SUM; ORDER DESC.
steps: Chain Customers-Orders-Payments.
Totals: Asha 1200, Ravi 400, Meena 2000.
HAVING SUM > 1000 keeps Asha, Meena (WHERE SUM impossible).
ORDER BY total_spent DESC: Meena, Asha.
insight: Mock of the real slot: 3 tables + GROUP + HAVING. WHERE-vs-HAVING decides it.
learn: Full pipeline: JOIN -> GROUP BY -> HAVING (aggregate) -> ORDER BY.

title: MOCK 2: Second-Highest Paid Dept (JOIN + Subquery)
statement: Tables Departments(id, dept_name), Employees(id, name, dept_id, salary). Show the dept_name with the second-highest average salary and its avg_sal (single row).
schemaSQL: CREATE TABLE Departments(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, dept_name TEXT); CREATE TABLE Employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept_id INTEGER, salary INTEGER);
seedSQL: INSERT INTO Departments VALUES (1,'Sales'),(2,'HR'),(3,'IT'); INSERT INTO Employees VALUES (1,'A',1,100),(2,'B',1,200),(3,'C',2,500),(4,'D',3,300),(5,'E',3,400);
hiddenSeedSQL: INSERT INTO Departments VALUES (10,'A'),(20,'B'); INSERT INTO Employees VALUES (30,'X',10,1000),(31,'Y',20,100);
solution: SELECT dept_name, avg_sal FROM (SELECT d.dept_name AS dept_name, AVG(e.salary) AS avg_sal FROM Departments d JOIN Employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id GROUP BY d.dept_name) ORDER BY avg_sal DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;
starter:
-- dept with 2nd-highest average salary
SELECT dept_name, avg_sal FROM (
SELECT d.dept_name AS dept_name, AVG(e.salary) AS avg_sal
FROM Departments d JOIN Employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.dept_name)
ORDER BY avg_sal DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;
approach: Inner aggregates avg per dept; outer orders and skips 1 (OFFSET 1) to land on second.
steps: Avgs: Sales 150, HR 500, IT 350.
ORDER DESC: HR 500, IT 350, Sales 150.
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 skips HR, takes IT 350.
Subquery-in-FROM (derived table) + outer ORDER/LIMIT.
insight: Derived table + ORDER + OFFSET = second-by-aggregate. Composes L2+L3 skills.
learn: Derived tables: aggregate inside, rank outside with ORDER BY + LIMIT/OFFSET.
